blocks.text: Intent classification fine-tuning trains a model to determine what a user is trying to accomplish with a given utterance, a specific application of the classification approach covered earlier in this module, most commonly used to route user requests within a conversational system.

This topic covers how intent differs from the sentiment task covered in the previous topic, the practical challenge of out-of-scope utterances, and why intent classification usually needs to work alongside entity extraction rather than in isolation.
1. What Intent Classification Targets

blocks.alt: A user utterance goes through an intent classifier, producing a predicted intent

blocks.text: Intent classification applies the general classification approach, covered in an earlier topic, to a label set representing distinct user goals or actions, "cancel my order" and "where is my order" express different intents even though both concern the same order.
2. Intent vs Sentiment

blocks.alt: Sentiment asks how someone feels while intent asks what someone wants

blocks.text: Sentiment analysis, covered in the previous topic, asks how someone feels about something, intent classification asks a different question entirely, what someone actually wants to accomplish, the two are often used together in a conversational system but they answer genuinely separate questions.
3. Designing an Intent Label Set

blocks.alt: check_order_status, cancel_order, request_refund, and a fallback intent form a label set

blocks.text: A well designed intent label set covers the distinct actions a system actually needs to route between, check_order_status, cancel_order, request_refund, and typically includes a fallback or other category for utterances that do not clearly match any defined intent, rather than forcing every input into one of the specific categories.

code.content:
{"utterance": "I want to cancel my order from yesterday",
 "intent": "cancel_order"}

blocks.text: 4. Intent Classification Alongside Entity Extraction

blocks.alt: A user utterance produces both an intent and extracted entities like order number or date

blocks.text: Knowing a user intent is cancel_order is rarely enough on its own, a production system typically also needs specific details, which order, entity extraction, closely related to the named entity recognition topic covered later in this module, usually runs alongside intent classification to pull out those specifics.

blocks.text: 5. Handling Out-of-Scope Utterances

blocks.alt: An in-scope intent is compared against an out of scope utterance needing a fallback

blocks.text: Real users will inevitably say things that do not match any defined intent, training data specifically including a diverse set of out-of-scope examples labeled as fallback teaches the model to recognize when to hand off to a human or ask a clarifying question, rather than confidently misclassifying an unrelated request into the nearest defined intent.

blocks.title: Skipping fallback data is a common early mistake
blocks.content: A model trained only on in-scope examples has no way to learn what out-of-scope looks like, and tends to force every input into whichever defined intent happens to be closest, producing confidently wrong routing decisions.

blocks.text: 6. Confusable Intents

blocks.alt: Similar phrased intents lead to confusion between intents

blocks.text: Intents with similar surface phrasing, "cancel my order" versus "cancel my subscription", are a common source of misclassification, reviewing a confusion matrix, covered in the general Classification topic, specifically for intent pairs that get confused helps identify where either the label definitions or the training data need refinement.
7. Intent Classification Driving Dialogue Flow

blocks.alt: An intent classification result drives dialogue system routing toward the appropriate response flow

blocks.text: In a conversational system, the predicted intent typically determines which downstream logic or response flow handles the rest of the interaction, making intent classification accuracy directly consequential, a misclassified intent routes the user into entirely the wrong flow, not just a slightly wrong response.
8. Evaluating Intent Classifiers

Beyond standard per-class precision and recall, covered in the general Classification topic, intent classifiers specifically benefit from testing a held out set of genuinely out-of-scope utterances, checking the fallback rate is neither too high, rejecting valid requests, nor too low, forcing invalid ones into a wrong intent.
9. Common Production Use Cases

Intent classification commonly powers customer support chatbots, voice assistants, and automated ticket routing systems, cases where correctly identifying what a user wants determines which specific workflow or team should handle the request next.
Worked Example

A team building a customer support chatbot defines ten intents covering their most common request types, plus a fallback category, and collects training examples for each, deliberately including a diverse set of out-of-scope utterances for the fallback category.

A confusion matrix review after initial training reveals cancel_order and request_refund are frequently confused, prompting the team to review both intent definitions and realize many training examples were ambiguously labeled between the two, relabeling those examples with clearer criteria noticeably improves the confusion rate on a follow up evaluation.
Common Mistakes

items: Training only on in-scope examples, leaving the model unable to recognize genuinely out-of-scope requests
Designing an intent label set with overlapping or ambiguous category definitions that confuse both labelers and the model
Treating intent classification as sufficient on its own without entity extraction to fill in the specific details needed
Not reviewing a confusion matrix to identify specific intent pairs that are frequently mixed up

blocks.text: Practice

For a conversational system you are familiar with, sketch five distinct intent categories plus a fallback category, write one example utterance for each, and identify one pair of intents from your list that might be easily confused, along with how you would clarify the distinction.
Key Takeaway

Intent classification determines what a user wants to accomplish, distinct from the sentiment task covered in the previous topic, and effective production systems need a well defined label set including a fallback category for out-of-scope utterances, usually paired with entity extraction to fill in the specific details a recognized intent still needs to be acted on.
